claim: Translation of aberrant mRNAs induces ribosomal collisions.
source: Translation of aberrant mRNAs induces ribosomal collisions, thereby triggering pathways for mRNA and nascent peptide degradation and ribosomal rescue.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that is supported by citations to prior work in the introduction.

claim: Ribosomal collisions trigger pathways for mRNA and nascent peptide degradation and ribosomal rescue.
source: Translation of aberrant mRNAs induces ribosomal collisions, thereby triggering pathways for mRNA and nascent peptide degradation and ribosomal rescue.
evidence: This statement is supported by extensive citations in the introduction describing quality control pathways.

claim: Sucrose gradient fractionation combined with quantitative proteomics can systematically identify proteins associated with collided ribosomes.
source: Here we use sucrose gradient fractionation combined with quantitative proteomics to systematically identify proteins associated with collided ribosomes.
evidence: This is the methodological approach described and demonstrated in the manuscript with experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: EDF1 is a novel protein recruited to collided ribosomes during translational distress.
source: This approach identified Endothelial differentiation-related factor 1 (EDF1) as a novel protein recruited to collided ribosomes during translational distress.
evidence: This is supported by the polysome proteomics data in Figure 1 and validation experiments in Figure 1I-K.

claim: EDF1 and its yeast homolog Mbf1 have a conserved 40S ribosomal subunit binding site at the mRNA entry channel near the collision interface.
source: Cryo-electron microscopic analyses of EDF1 and its yeast homolog Mbf1 revealed a conserved 40S ribosomal subunit binding site at the mRNA entry channel near the collision interface.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structures presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: EDF1 recruits the translational repressors GIGYF2 and EIF4E2 to collided ribosomes.
source: EDF1 recruits the translational repressors GIGYF2 and EIF4E2 to collided ribosomes to initiate a negative-feedback loop that prevents new ribosomes from translating defective mRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by the polysome proteomics data in Figure 6, immunoblotting in Figure 6D, and functional assays in Figure 6E.

claim: EDF1-dependent recruitment of GIGYF2 and EIF4E2 initiates a negative-feedback loop that prevents new ribosomes from translating defective mRNAs.
source: EDF1 recruits the translational repressors GIGYF2 and EIF4E2 to collided ribosomes to initiate a negative-feedback loop that prevents new ribosomes from translating defective mRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by the reporter assays in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2H showing increased translation in the absence of EDF1 or GIGYF2/EIF4E2.

claim: EDF1 regulates an immediate-early transcriptional response to ribosomal collisions.
source: Further, EDF1 regulates an immediate-early transcriptional response to ribosomal collisions.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data in Figure 7 showing EDF1-dependent transcriptional changes in response to emetine treatment.

claim: Low doses of translational elongation inhibitors induce global ribosomal collisions.
source: Previous studies reported that global ribosome-collisions can be induced using low, but not high, doses of translational elongation inhibitors such as cycloheximide, anisomycin and emetine (Juszkiewicz et al., 2018; Simms et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and validated in the manuscript with RNase A digestion experiments in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment with 1.8 µM emetine for 15 min induces transcriptome-wide ribosomal collisions in HCT116 cells.
source: In untreated cells, the majority of polysomes collapsed into monosomes upon RNase A treatment, while in cells treated with low doses of emetine (1.8 µM, 15 min), we observed a significant increase in the fraction of nuclease-resistant disomes (2°) and trisomes (3°).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RNase A digestion experiment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ASCC3 and ZNF598 are enriched in denser polysomal fractions in cells treated with low-dose emetine compared to untreated cells.
source: As anticipated, in cells treated with low-dose emetine (EL), compared to untreated cells (UT), ASCC3 and ZNF598 were enriched in denser polysomal fractions (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblotting of sucrose gradient fractions in Figure 1B.

claim: A total of 4288 proteins were quantified across all fractions in the polysome proteomics experiment.
source: We quantified a total of 4288 proteins across all fractions (Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: This is stated in the results and the data is provided in the source data file.

claim: 79 of the 80 annotated ribosomal proteins were quantified in the polysome proteomics experiment.
source: We quantified a total of 4288 proteins across all fractions (Figure 1—source data 1); 79 of the 80 annotated r-proteins were quantified with the exception being RPL41/eL41 which is small (3.5 kilodaltons) and has no tryptic peptides of sufficient length for detection.
evidence: This is stated in the results with an explanation for the missing protein.

claim: RPL41/eL41 was not quantified because it is small (3.5 kilodaltons) and has no tryptic peptides of sufficient length for detection.
source: 79 of the 80 annotated r-proteins were quantified with the exception being RPL41/eL41 which is small (3.5 kilodaltons) and has no tryptic peptides of sufficient length for detection.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the properties of the protein and the mass spectrometry method used.

claim: Ribosomal proteins showed no enrichment in the ribonucleoprotein (RNP) fractions between emetine-treated and untreated samples.
source: Consistent with the profiles of the A260 traces (Figure 1C), mapped r-proteins between emetine-treated and untreated samples showed no enrichment in the ribonucleoprotein (RNP) fractions (log2(EL/UT)~0; fractions 1–2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1N)
evidence: This is shown in the volcano plots and line plots in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ribosomal proteins showed de-enrichment along the monosomal fractions in emetine-treated samples compared to untreated samples.
source: mapped r-proteins between emetine-treated and untreated samples showed no enrichment in the ribonucleoprotein (RNP) fractions (log2(EL/UT)~0; fractions 1–2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1N), de-enrichment along the monosomal fractions (log2(EL/UT)<0; fractions 4–5; Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1N)
evidence: This is shown in the volcano plots and line plots in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ribosomal proteins showed progressive enrichment along the light and heavy polysomal fractions in emetine-treated samples compared to untreated samples.
source: mapped r-proteins between emetine-treated and untreated samples showed no enrichment in the ribonucleoprotein (RNP) fractions (log2(EL/UT)~0; fractions 1–2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1N), de-enrichment along the monosomal fractions (log2(EL/UT)<0; fractions 4–5; Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1N), and progressive enrichment along the light and heavy polysomal fractions (log2(EL/UT)>0; fractions 6–10; Figure 1—figure supplement 1H–1L, Figure 1—figure supplement 1N).
evidence: This is shown in the volcano plots and line plots in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: LARP1, PABPC4, STAU1, and UPF1 followed the overall abundance profile of ribosomal proteins.
source: Known ribosome-binding proteins or those typically associated with ribosome-bound mRNAs followed the overall abundance profile of r-proteins (shown for LARP1, PABPC4, STAU1, and UPF1) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1O).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1O.

claim: EIF5B is preferentially enriched in the monosomal fractions but not polysomal fractions upon emetine treatment.
source: Proteins that function on distinct ribosomal subcomplexes are also revealed, such as the late stage initiation factor EIF5B which is preferentially enriched in the monosomal (fractions 4–5) but not polysomal fractions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1O).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1O.

claim: NEMF and EIF6 were enriched in the monosomal fractions as a function of emetine treatment.
source: For example, a few known components of the ribosome-mediated QC machinery such as NEMF and EIF6 were enriched in the monosomal fractions as a function of emetine (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–1G, log2(EL/UT)>0; Figure 1—figure supplement 1P)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F-G and 1P.

claim: LARP1 and UPF1 followed the abundance profile of ribosomal proteins in monosomal fractions.
source: while cognate ribosome-binding proteins such as LARP1 and UPF1 simply followed the abundance profile of r-proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–G, log2(EL/UT)<0; Figure 1—figure supplement 1P).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F-G and 1P.

claim: GIGYF2 and EIF4E2 showed little to no enrichment in the lighter fractions, but were substantially enriched in the heavier polysomal fractions upon emetine treatment.
source: Notably, the cap-dependent translational repressors GIGYF2 and EIF4E2 showed little to no enrichment in the lighter fractions, but were substantially enriched in the heavier polysomal fractions
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F.

claim: TRIP4 and ASCC3 accumulated along polysomes in an emetine-dependent manner.
source: similar trends were observed for the ribosome-associated protein quality control (RQC) trigger complex (RQT complex), including components TRIP4 and ASCC3.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F.

claim: NEMF and VCP accumulated along polysomes in an emetine-dependent manner.
source: The late stage RQC components, NEMF and VCP, also accumulated along polysomes in an emetine-dependent manner.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F.

claim: G3BP1 was enriched specifically in the 40S fraction of emetine treated samples.
source: Interestingly, G3BP1, a component of the USP10 deubiquitylase (DUB) complex that removes ubiquitylation marks on eS10 post ribosomal splitting (Meyer et al., 2020), was enriched specifically in the 40S fraction of emetine treated samples (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F and is consistent with the known function of G3BP1 cited from Meyer et al., 2020.

claim: EDF1, NACA, BTF3 and TCOF1 were particularly enriched (more than 2-fold) in polysomal fractions of emetine-treated samples.
source: A subset of proteins was particularly enriched (more than 2-fold in terms of fold change) in polysomal fractions of emetine-treated samples (Figure 1E, Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1H–1L). The exemplary candidates in this list were EDF1, NACA, BTF3 and TCOF1.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E, 1G, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H-L.

claim: TCOF1 (Treacle protein) is a known substrate of the E3 ubiquitin (Ub) ligase CUL3 that regulates the pseudo-uridylation status of ribosomal RNA.
source: TCOF1 (Treacle protein) is a known substrate of the E3 ubiquitin (Ub) ligase CUL3 that regulates the pseudo-uridylation status of ribosomal RNA (Werner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Werner et al., 2015.

claim: NACA and BTF3 bind nascent polypeptide chains emerging from the exit tunnel and prevent their mistargeting to the endoplasmic reticulum by the signal recognition particle (SRP) complex.
source: NACA (nascent polypeptide-associated complex subunit alpha) and its binding partner BTF3 (basic transcription factor 3) bind nascent polypeptide chains emerging from the exit tunnel and prevents their mistargeting to the endoplasmic reticulum by the signal recognition particle (SRP) complex (Gamerdinger et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gamerdinger et al., 2019.

claim: NACA/BTF3 function as transcriptional coactivators that regulate the activity of JUN during various differentiation programs.
source: Additionally, NACA/BTF3 also function as transcriptional coactivators that regulate the activity of JUN during various differentiation programs (Addison et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Addison et al., 2019.

claim: EDF1 was the most enriched protein in heavy polysome fractions of emetine-treated samples.
source: We focused our attention on EDF1 because it was the most enriched protein in heavy polysome fractions of emetine-treated samples (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1H–1L, Figure 1—figure supplement 1O).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H-L and 1O.

claim: The yeast homolog of EDF1, Mbf1, was implicated in preventing ribosomal frameshifting on iterated rare codon stretches known to trigger ribosome-mediated QC pathways.
source: Importantly, previous genetic studies had implicated its yeast homolog Mbf1 in preventing ribosomal frameshifting on iterated rare codon stretches known to trigger ribosome-mediated QC pathways (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2018.

claim: EDF1 was unable to be detected on 40S, 60S and 80S fractions in the polysome proteomics data.
source: We were unable to detect EDF1 on 40S, 60S and 80S fractions, but saw strong enrichment ([EL/UT]~7–10) on polysome fractions of emetine-treated samples (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1O).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1O.

claim: EDF1 showed strong enrichment ([EL/UT]~7–10) on polysome fractions of emetine-treated samples.
source: We were unable to detect EDF1 on 40S, 60S and 80S fractions, but saw strong enrichment ([EL/UT]~7–10) on polysome fractions of emetine-treated samples (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1O).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1O.

claim: EDF1 was barely present in polysomes of untreated cells.
source: We compared the enrichment pattern of EDF1 to the cohort of r-proteins (shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1O) – these analyses indicated that EDF1 was barely present in polysomes of untreated cells ([EDF1UT, polysomes] << [EDF1EL, polysomes] resulting in high EDF1 [EL/UT] ratios).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1O.

claim: EDF1 was strongly recruited to polysomes of cells treated with low doses of anisomycin (0.19 µM, 15 min).
source: To test if EDF1 recruitment to polysomes was specific to elongation stalls promoted by emetine, we treated cells with low doses of a distinct elongation inhibitor, anisomycin (0.19 µM, 15 min), and again observed strong recruitment of EDF1 to polysomes (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblotting in Figure 1J.

claim: Pyrimidine dimers accumulate in mRNAs of UV-irradiated cells and impede the decoding step of translational elongation leading to transcriptome-wide ribosome collisions.
source: Recent observations indicate that pyrimidine dimers accumulate in mRNAs of UV-irradiated cells and impede the decoding step of translational elongation leading to transcriptome-wide ribosome collisions (Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2020.

claim: EDF1 was robustly recruited to polysomes in UV-irradiated cells.
source: Indeed, compared to untreated cells, polysomal fractionation of UV-irradiated cells revealed robust recruitment of EDF1 (Figure 1K) despite the overall diminished polysome abundance resulting from activation of the Integrated Stress Response (ISR) (Collier et al., 2015; Higgins et al., 2015).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblotting in Figure 1K.

claim: ZNF598 (Hel2 in yeast) catalyzes site-specific ubiquitylation of eS10 and uS10 at the collided ribosomal interface.
source: ZNF598 (Hel2 in yeast) is an early-acting ribosome-mediated QC factor that catalyzes site-specific ubiquitylation of eS10 and uS10 at the collided ribosomal interface (Juszkiewicz et al., 2018; Juszkiewicz and Hegde, 2017; Matsuo et al., 2017; Simms et al., 2017; Sundaramoorthy et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Hel2 in yeast acts upstream of the endonuclease Cue2 (N4BP2 in mammals), which catalyzes the degradation of problematic mRNAs.
source: For example, Hel2 in yeast was shown to act upstream of the endonuclease Cue2 (N4BP2 in mammals), which contains four putative ubiquitin binding domains (including the namesake CUE for coupling of ubiquitin binding to ER degradation), and catalyzes the degradation of problematic mRNAs (D'Orazio et al., 2019; Ikeuchi et al., 2019; Simms et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to D'Orazio et al., 2019; Ikeuchi et al., 2019; Simms et al., 2017.

claim: Cue2 (N4BP2 in mammals) contains four putative ubiquitin binding domains including the CUE domain.
source: For example, Hel2 in yeast was shown to act upstream of the endonuclease Cue2 (N4BP2 in mammals), which contains four putative ubiquitin binding domains (including the namesake CUE for coupling of ubiquitin binding to ER degradation), and catalyzes the degradation of problematic mRNAs (D'Orazio et al., 2019; Ikeuchi et al., 2019; Simms et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CUE domains are present in Cue3 (ASCC2 in mammals) which is a part of the trimeric RQT complex.
source: CUE domains are also present in Cue3 (ASCC2 in mammals) which is a part of the trimeric RQT complex (along with yKR023W and Slh1; known as TRIP4 and ASCC3 respectively in mammals) that promotes dissociation of collided ribosomes (Matsuo et al., 2020; Matsuo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Matsuo et al., 2020; Matsuo et al., 2017.

claim: The RQT complex promotes dissociation of collided ribosomes.
source: CUE domains are also present in Cue3 (ASCC2 in mammals) which is a part of the trimeric RQT complex (along with yKR023W and Slh1; known as TRIP4 and ASCC3 respectively in mammals) that promotes dissociation of collided ribosomes (Matsuo et al., 2020; Matsuo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Matsuo et al., 2020; Matsuo et al., 2017.

claim: Ltn1-mediated nascent peptide degradation is compromised in yeast carrying ubiquitin binding mutants of Cue3.
source: While Ltn1-mediated nascent peptide degradation is compromised in yeast carrying ubiquitin binding mutants of Cue3 (Matsuo et al., 2017), whether the recruitment of the RQT complex is dependent on Hel2-mediated ubiquitination events is currently unclear (Juszkiewicz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Matsuo et al., 2017.

claim: ZNF598 associates with the cap-dependent translational initiation repressor EIF4E2 through its binding to GIGYF2.
source: Finally, in mammals, ZNF598 was previously shown to associate with the cap-dependent translational initiation repressor EIF4E2 (also called 4EHP) through its binding to the Grb10-interacting GYF protein 2 (GIGYF2) (Garzia et al., 2017; Tollenaere et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Garzia et al., 2017; Tollenaere et al., 2019.

claim: Recruitment of EDF1 to collided ribosomes is ZNF598 independent.
source: Surprisingly, we noticed that the recruitment of most proteins, including known ribosome-mediated QC factors, to emetine-dependent collided ribosomes occurred in the absence of ZNF598 (log2[ΔZNF598(EL/UT)] > 0, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B). Among these, EDF1 was the most enriched protein accumulating on polysomes of emetine-treated WT, ΔZNF598, and ZNF598-OE cell lines (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C-F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The enrichment of EDF1 to collided ribosomes was unperturbed in the absence of ZNF598, or upon ZNF598 overexpression.
source: Using this analysis, we found that the enrichment of EDF1 to collided ribosomes was unperturbed in the absence of ZNF598, or upon ZNF598 overexpression (Figure 2D-E, enrichment value ≥ 0).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Emetine-dependent accumulation of EDF1 on polysomes occurs in ΔZNF598 cells.
source: We further validated these results by immunoblot analyses of fractionated lysates from untreated or low dose emetine treated (1.8 µM, 15 min) ΔZNF598 cells, which showed emetine-dependent accumulation of EDF1 on polysomes (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblotting in Figure 2F.

claim: The recruitment of GIGYF2, TRIP4, ASCC3, PELO, HBS1L and N4BP2 to collided ribosomes was largely unperturbed in ΔZNF598 and ZNF598-OE cells.
source: Interestingly, our enrichment analysis also revealed that the recruitment of known ribosome-mediated QC factors (such as GIGYF2, TRIP4, ASCC3, PELO, HBS1L and N4BP2), some with known Ub-binding domains, to collided ribosomes was largely unperturbed (enrichment value ≥ 0) in ΔZNF598 and ZNF598-OE cells (Figure 2D-E, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Loss of EDF1 decreases emetine-stimulated ubiquitylation of eS10 and uS10.
source: To test whether loss of EDF1 disrupts ubiquitylation of eS10 and uS10, we treated HEK293T cells with non-targeting (SCR) or EDF1-targeting siRNAs (EDF1i), without (UT, 0 µM) or with low dose emetine (EL, 1.8 µM, 15 min). We observed that depletion of EDF1 decreased emetine-stimulated ubiquitylation of eS10 and uS10 (Figure 2G, compare lane 2 to lane 4).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblotting in Figure 2G.

claim: EDF1 depletion decreased the amount of mono- and di-ubiquitylated eS10 on polysomes.
source: To ensure that the effects on eS10 and uS10 ubiquitylation were specific to collisions, we separated cell lysates from non-targeting (SCR) or EDF1 siRNA treated samples, with (EL, 1.8 µM, 15 min) or without (UT, 0 µM) emetine treatment across 10–50% sucrose gradients. Consistent with our results from whole cell extracts, immunoblotting of pooled monosome and polysome fractions showed that EDF1 depletion decreased the amount of mono- and di-ubiquitylated eS10 on polysomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblotting in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: ΔEDF1 cell clones showed a modest decrease in eS10 and uS10 ubiquitylation after UV treatment compared to WT cells.
source: Compared to untreated cells, parental (HEK293 Flp-In WT) cell lines showed an increase in eS10 and uS10 ubiquitylation after UV treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, compare lane 1 to lane 2); however, compared to WT cells, all three ΔEDF1 cell clones showed a modest decrease in eS10 and uS10 ubiquitylation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, compare lane 2 to lanes 4, 6 and 8).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblotting in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Ubiquitylation of eS10 at K138/139 was decreased in ΔEDF1 cells compared to WT cells following low-dose emetine treatment.
source: Consistent with results obtained from immunoblotting, ubiquitylation of eS10 at K138/139 was decreased in ΔEDF1 cells compared to WT cells following low-dose emetine treatment (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is shown by TMT-based quantification in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Loss of EDF1 resulted in a modest (~10–20%) decrease in the recruitment of ZNF598 to polysomes in response to emetine treatment.
source: To test whether loss of EDF1 impacted the collision-dependent recruitment of ZNF598 to polysomes, we quantified ZNF598 recruitment to polysomes of WT and ΔEDF1 cells in response to emetine treatment and observed a modest (~10–20%) decrease in the recruitment of ZNF598 in cells lacking EDF1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G, [{ΔEDF1(EL/UT)}/{WT(EL/UT)}]<1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2G.

claim: The emetine-stimulated increase in phospho-p38 level was reduced upon partial depletion of EDF1 with siRNAs compared to WT cells.
source: Recent studies have shown that the MAPKKK ZAKα recognizes collided ribosomes to trigger the stress-activated signaling cascade by phosphorylation of p38 and JNKs (Wu et al., 2020). We find that compared to WT cells, the emetine-stimulated increase in phospho-p38 level was reduced upon partial depletion of EDF1 with siRNAs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblotting in Figure 2—figure supplement 2H.

claim: Emetine-dependent EDF1 accumulation on polysomes was compromised in RACK1 depleted cells.
source: HCT116 cells were treated with non-targeting (SCR) or RACK1-specific siRNAs, without or with low-dose emetine (1.8 µM, 15 min), lysed and resolved across 10–50% sucrose gradients. Treatment with RACK1-specific siRNAs did not distort the distribution of polysomes as shown by the A260 traces or RPL10A distribution across the non-targeting (SCR) and RACK1i sucrose gradients (Figure 2I). However, emetine-dependent EDF1 accumulation on polysomes was compromised in the RACK1 depleted cells (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblotting in Figure 2I.

claim: RACK1 is critical for EDF1 recruitment to collided ribosomes, either directly or through its role in stabilizing the collision interface.
source: These results indicate that RACK1 either directly or through its role in stabilizing the collision interface is critical for EDF1 recruitment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The structure of a non-rotated ribosomal complex showing extra density near the mRNA entry tunnel and in the ribosomal A site was determined at an average resolution of 2.9 Å.
source: After 3D classification (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), the structure of a non-rotated ribosomal complex showing extra density near the mRNA entry tunnel and in the ribosomal A site was determined at an average resolution of 2.9 Å (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–1E top panels).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in the figures.

claim: The density in the A site of the EDF1-bound ribosome was identified as the cell growth-regulating nucleolar protein LYAR.
source: Whereas the density in the A site was identified as the cell growth-regulating nucleolar protein LYAR, the density near the mRNA entry channel belonged to EDF1, for which a near complete molecular model was built from residues Ser-24 to Arg-133 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A near complete molecular model of EDF1 was built from residues Ser-24 to Arg-133.
source: Whereas the density in the A site was identified as the cell growth-regulating nucleolar protein LYAR, the density near the mRNA entry channel belonged to EDF1, for which a near complete molecular model was built from residues Ser-24 to Arg-133 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mbf1 was found occupying the same position on the ribosome as EDF1 at an average resolution of 3.2 Å.
source: In stalled trisomes isolated from this system, we observed Mbf1 occupying the same position on the ribosome at an average resolution of 3.2 Å (Figure 3B–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–1E bottom panels, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in the figures.

claim: Mbf1 was found associated with the collided ribosome which adopted a rotated state with hybrid tRNAs in the A/P and P/E positions.
source: Although Mbf1 was found associated with the collided ribosome which adopted a rotated state with hybrid tRNAs in the A/P and P/E positions (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), EDF1 and Mbf1 displayed identical structures and modes of binding (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: EDF1 and Mbf1 displayed identical structures and modes of binding.
source: Although Mbf1 was found associated with the collided ribosome which adopted a rotated state with hybrid tRNAs in the A/P and P/E positions (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), EDF1 and Mbf1 displayed identical structures and modes of binding (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: The conformation of the 40S subunit itself is indistinguishable between the non-rotated state of the EDF1 complex and the rotated state of the Mbf1 complex.
source: These observations are consistent with the fact that the conformation of the 40S subunit itself is indistinguishable between the non-rotated state of the EDF1 complex and the rotated state of the Mbf1 complex (Matsuo et al., 2020; Tesina et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations to Matsuo et al., 2020; Tesina et al., 2020.

claim: The C-terminal helix-turn-helix (HTH)-domain of EDF1 and Mbf1 is sandwiched between helix 33 (h33) and helix 16 (h16) of the 18S ribosomal RNA (rRNA).
source: In these structures, the C-terminal helix-turn-helix (HTH)-domain of both proteins is sandwiched between helix 33 (h33) and helix 16 (h16) of the 18S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) with h16 being displaced from its normal position towards EDF1/Mbf1 by about five degrees (Figure 3D, Figure 3E, bottom left and right).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: Helix 16 (h16) of the 18S rRNA is displaced from its normal position towards EDF1/Mbf1 by about five degrees.
source: In these structures, the C-terminal helix-turn-helix (HTH)-domain of both proteins is sandwiched between helix 33 (h33) and helix 16 (h16) of the 18S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) with h16 being displaced from its normal position towards EDF1/Mbf1 by about five degrees (Figure 3D, Figure 3E, bottom left and right).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: EDF1 and Mbf1 extend along the mRNA entry channel, interacting prominently with conserved residues of the ribosomal protein uS3.
source: EDF1 and Mbf1 then extend along the mRNA entry channel, interacting prominently with conserved residues of the ribosomal protein uS3 (Figure 3D, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3D and Figure 4A.

claim: Most of the conserved residues in uS3 interacting with EDF1 and Mbf1 were previously shown to be required for inhibition of frameshifting on stall-inducing iterated CGA codons.
source: Interestingly, most of the conserved residues in uS3 interacting with EDF1 and Mbf1 were previously shown to be required for inhibition of frameshifting on stall-inducing iterated CGA codons (Wang et al., 2018), underlining the functional significance of the observed architecture in this region in close proximity to the mRNA (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2018.

claim: An N-terminal alpha-helix of EDF1/Mbf1 interacts with h16 and the r-proteins uS4 and eS30.
source: From uS3, EDF1 and Mbf1 reach down to the base of rRNA h16, where an N-terminal alpha-helix of EDF1/Mbf1 interacts with h16 and the r-proteins uS4 and eS30 (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: Binding of EDF1 and Mbf1 displaces the C-terminus of eS30 which normally interacts with rRNA helix 18 (h18).
source: Binding of EDF1 and Mbf1 displaces the C-terminus of eS30 which normally interacts with rRNA helix 18 (h18) (Figure 3E, top four panels).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: EDF1 interacts with h18 through a GQNKQ-motif, thereby mimicking the interaction of the displaced C-terminus of eS30.
source: EDF1 itself interacts with h18 through a GQNKQ-motif, thereby mimicking the interaction of the displaced C-terminus of eS30 (GPNAN).
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: In its canonical conformation, the C-terminus of eS30 forms a loop which would clash with the re-positioned h16 in the EDF1- and Mbf1-bound ribosomes.
source: In its canonical conformation, the C-terminus of eS30 forms a loop which would now clash with the re-positioned h16 in the EDF1- and Mbf1-bound ribosomes (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Lysine 43 (K43) of EDF1 points towards the phosphate backbone of h16 and reaches over the eS30 helix, thereby preventing eS30 from maintaining its canonical conformation.
source: In addition, lysine 43 (K43) of EDF1 points towards the phosphate backbone of h16 and reaches over the eS30 helix formed by residues extending from glycine 30 to arginine 42, thereby preventing eS30 from maintaining its canonical conformation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The KKW42-44 motif of EDF1 (KKY46-48 in Mbf1) is ideally positioned to interact with the mRNA in the entry channel.
source: Interestingly, the stretch linking the N-terminal alpha-helix of EDF1/Mbf1 on h16 with the h18/uS3 interaction site contains a conserved KKW42-44 motif (KKY46-48 in Mbf1), with the aromatic residue ideally positioned to interact with the mRNA in the entry channel.
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: Y48 of Mbf1 directly interacts with the mRNA.
source: While the mammalian immunopurified EDF1-bound ribosomes lacked visible mRNA, in the Mbf1-bound ribosomes we followed the mRNA density from the E site to the mRNA entry channel near h16 (Figure 4B) where Mbf1's KKY46-48 motif positions Y48 of Mbf1 to directly interact with the mRNA (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The KKY motif and the following alpha-helix clamp the mRNA, resembling a headlock-like arrangement.
source: The KKY motif is followed immediately by an alpha-helix and together these structural entities clamp the mRNA, resembling a headlock-like arrangement (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In the presence of Mbf1, the mRNA follows a path which is distinct from the mRNA path in collided ribosomes in the absence of Mbf1.
source: This notion of an mRNA headlock provided by EDF1/Mbf1 is further supported by the observation that in the presence of Mbf1, the mRNA follows a path which is distinct from the mRNA path in collided ribosomes in the absence of Mbf1 (Figure 4D; Matsuo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Mbf1 was exclusively bound to collided ribosomes found in the rotated state.
source: Notably, when analysing the Mbf1 occupancy of individual ribosomes we observed that Mbf1 was exclusively bound to collided ribosomes found in the rotated state (Figure 4E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Mbf1 was not found in the first stalled ribosome, which is found in a non-rotated canonical post state.
source: We did not find Mbf1 in the first stalled ribosome, which in the case of the SDD1 mRNA, is found in a non-rotated canonical post state.
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: Mbf1 is present in both the first and the second collided ribosome, with a slight preference for the second one.
source: Moreover, by analysis of neighboring ribosomes, we found that Mbf1 is present in both the first and the second collided ribosome, with a slight preference for the second one (Figure 4E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: EDF1 and Mbf1 are more likely to be recruited to trailing ribosomes following the initial stalling event.
source: We conclude that EDF1 and Mbf1 are more likely to be recruited to trailing ribosomes following the initial stalling event.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data on Mbf1 occupancy.

claim: The abnormally long-lived rotated state of the collided ribosome may serve as a molecular cue for Mbf1/EDF1 recruitment.
source: The abnormally long-lived rotated state of the collided ribosome, which is unable to complete the tRNA-mRNA translocation step, may serve as a molecular cue for Mbf1/EDF1 recruitment.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that Mbf1 binds to rotated ribosomes.

claim: The highly conserved N-terminus of Mbf1/EDF1 may play a role in sensing neighboring ribosomes after collision.
source: We speculate that the highly conserved N-terminus of Mbf1/EDF1, which is delocalized in our structures, may play a role in sensing neighboring ribosomes after collision and thus in specific recruitment to colliding ribosomes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural data.

claim: TCOF1, GIGYF2 and EIF4E2 were identified as strong EDF1-interacting proteins by immunoaffinity purification.
source: MS analysis of IP eluates identified TCOF1 along with the translational repressors GIGYF2 and EIF4E2 as strong EDF1-interacting proteins (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ZNF598 and components of the RQT complex were identified as EDF1-interacting proteins by immunoaffinity purification.
source: Other ribosome-mediated QC factors were also identified including ZNF598 and components of the RQT complex, as well as kinases (mTOR, casein kinase II (CKII), and ribosomal protein S6 kinase (RPS6K)) involved in the phosphorylation of r-proteins (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: An interaction between EDF1 and N4BP2 is greatly enhanced under conditions that induce ribosomal collisions (1.8 µM emetine).
source: Interestingly, we find that an interaction between EDF1 and N4BP2 is greatly enhanced under conditions that induce ribosomal collisions (1.8 µM emetine) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: GIGYF2, EIF4E2, and TCOF1 were among the most significantly enriched proteins in EDF1-BioID analysis.
source: Consistent with results obtained from the EDF1 affinity purification, our EDF1-BioID analysis showed that the translational repressors GIGYF2•EIF4E2 along with TCOF1 were among the most significantly enriched proteins (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Recruitment of GIGYF2 and EIF4E2 to heavy polysomal fractions of emetine-treated samples strongly depended on EDF1.
source: Among these, we see that the recruitment of GIGYF2 and EIF4E2 to heavy polysomal fractions of emetine-treated samples strongly depended on EDF1 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C.

claim: GIGYF2 preferentially accumulated in heavier polysomes of emetine-treated WT cells.
source: GIGYF2 preferentially accumulated in heavier polysomes of emetine-treated WT cells (Figure 6D, left panel)
evidence: This is shown by immunoblotting in Figure 6D.

claim: GIGYF2 was not detected in emetine-treated polysomes of ΔEDF1 cells.
source: moreover, GIGYF2 was not detected in emetine-treated polysomes of ΔEDF1 cells (Figure 6D, right panel).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblotting in Figure 6D.

claim: Loss of EDF1 resulted in a significant increase in GFP fluorescence from the polyA-mediated stalling reporter compared to parental cells.
source: If EDF1 recruits GIGYF2•EIF4E2 to collided ribosomes, then its depletion should increase the bulk translational output (as reflected by overall GFP levels) of the polyA-mediated stalling reporter. Indeed, consistent with such a role, loss of EDF1 resulted in a significant increase in GFP fluorescence compared to parental cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6E.

claim: GIGYF2•EIF4E2 depletion resulted in an increase in GFP fluorescence from the polyA-mediated stalling reporter.
source: Similarly, GIGYF2•EIF4E2 depletion resulted in the expected increase in GFP fluorescence (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6E.

claim: GIGYF2•EIF4E2 depletion only mildly augmented the already increased GFP levels in ΔEDF1 cells.
source: Moreover, GIGYF2•EIF4E2 depletion only mildly augmented the already increased GFP levels in ΔEDF1 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: Restoring EDF1 in ΔEDF1 cells reduced GFP levels from the polyA-mediated stalling reporter.
source: Restoring EDF1 in ΔEDF1 cells reduced GFP levels whereas expression of truncated versions of EDF1 lacking either the N-terminal MBF1 or the C-terminal HTH domain failed to reduce the elevated GFP levels observed in ΔEDF1 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Expression of truncated versions of EDF1 lacking either the N-terminal MBF1 or the C-terminal HTH domain failed to reduce the elevated GFP levels observed in ΔEDF1 cells.
source: Restoring EDF1 in ΔEDF1 cells reduced GFP levels whereas expression of truncated versions of EDF1 lacking either the N-terminal MBF1 or the C-terminal HTH domain failed to reduce the elevated GFP levels observed in ΔEDF1 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The inability of EDF1 truncations to restore translational repression is due to defective ribosome binding.
source: The inability of EDF1 truncations to restore translational repression is due to defective ribosome binding (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–2C) consistent with our structural data (Figures 3–4) showing that both domains are required for 40S association.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B-C and is consistent with the structural data.

claim: No significant change in GFP was observed upon loss of ZNF598 in the polyA-mediated stalling reporter assay.
source: By contrast, no significant change in GFP was observed upon loss of ZNF598 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Loss of neither EDF1 nor GIGYF2•EIF4E2 affected the bulk translational output of an identical GFP-RFP reporter without the intervening polyA-stalling sequence.
source: Importantly, loss of neither EDF1 nor GIGYF2•EIF4E2 affected the bulk translational output of an identical GFP-RFP reporter without the intervening polyA-stalling sequence (Figure 6—figure supplement 2F for relative GFP intensity, Figure 6—figure supplement 2G for RFP:GFP ratios).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2F-G.

claim: Loss of EDF1, but not ZNF598, led to an increase in the bulk translation output on a reporter with an unspliced Xbp1 mRNA (Xbp1u) peptide-pausing sequence.
source: In an orthogonal set of reporter experiments, loss of EDF1, but not ZNF598, led to an increase in the bulk translation output (as measured by a significant increase in Renilla luciferase (RLuc) activity) on a reporter with an unspliced Xbp1 mRNA (Xbp1u) peptide-pausing sequence (Shanmuganathan et al., 2019; Yanagitani et al., 2011) previously reported to trigger ribosome collisions (Han et al., 2020; Figure 6—figure supplement 2H for relative RLuc activity, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2I for Fluc:RLuc ratios).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2H-I.

claim: EDF1 was identified as an evolutionarily conserved transcriptional coactivator that initiates transcriptional reprogramming in response to cellular stresses.
source: Previous studies identified EDF1 as an evolutionarily conserved transcriptional coactivator that initiates transcriptional reprogramming in response to cellular stresses (Baltz et al., 2012; Jaimes-Miranda and Chávez Montes, 2020; Jindra et al., 2004; Kabe et al., 1999; Takemaru et al., 1998; Takemaru et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: In flies and in mammals, EDF1 was shown to bind the protein product of the jun locus, JUN/AP-1, to mount a transcriptional response during oxidative stress.
source: For example, in flies and in mammals, EDF1 was shown to bind the protein product of the jun locus, JUN/AP-1, to mount a transcriptional response during oxidative stress (Jindra et al., 2004; Miotto and Struhl, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jindra et al., 2004; Miotto and Struhl, 2006.

claim: JUN is regulated through a positive feedback loop to mount a sustained cellular response.
source: Importantly, while there are many JUN transcriptional targets that respond to various JUN/AP-1 complexes, a well-characterized target is jun itself which is regulated through a positive feedback loop to mount a sustained cellular response (Angel et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Angel et al., 1988.

claim: The phosphorylation of JUN (at Ser 73) phenocopied the eS10 ubiquitylation dose-response to emetine treatment.
source: As anticipated, we observed maximal ubiquitylation of eS10 at intermediate but not high concentrations of emetine (Figure 7A). Additionally, we observed that the phosphorylation of JUN (at Ser 73) phenocopied the eS10 ubiquitylation dose-response, consistent with a model where JUN is activated in response to ribosomal collisions (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblotting in Figure 7A.

claim: A striking and progressive increase in the transcript abundance of JUN was observed following low-dose emetine treatment at 30 and 120 min by ~4 and ~8 fold respectively.
source: We observed a striking and progressive increase in the transcript abundance of JUN following low-dose emetine treatment at 30 and 120 min by ~4 and~8 fold respectively (Figure 7C–D, Figure 7F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C-D and 7F.

claim: Increased expression of FOS, EGR1, ATF3, TXNIP and DUSP1 was observed in response to low-dose emetine treatment.
source: We also observed increased expression of other transcripts including FOS, EGR1, ATF3, TXNIP and DUSP1, all transcriptional and signaling regulators that function in diverse stress response pathways (Figure 7C–D; Abraham and Clark, 2006; Chen et al., 1996; p. 3; Chiu et al., 1988; Halazonetis et al., 1988; Khachigian et al., 1996, p. 1; Slack et al., 2001).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C-D and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A relatively small collection of genes showed strong dependence on EDF1 in their emetine-induced transcriptional upregulation.
source: At both early and late time points, we found that a relatively small collection of genes showed strong dependence on EDF1 (Figure 7E–F, log2(fold change)<0 and -log padj >2, corresponding to the upper left quadrant of the plots).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7E-F.

claim: JUN, ATF3, DUSP1 and EGR1 showed robust transcriptional upregulation in response to ribosomal collisions in WT cells and strong dependence on EDF1.
source: Strikingly, these included the same cohort of genes (JUN, ATF3, DUSP1 and EGR1) that showed robust transcriptional upregulation in response to ribosomal collisions in WT cells (Figure 7E–F)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7E-F.

claim: JUND, FOS and FOSB showed somewhat less strong dependence on EDF1 for their emetine-induced transcriptional upregulation.
source: somewhat less strong dependence on EDF1 was also observed for JUND, FOS and FOSB (Figure 7E–F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7E-F.

claim: There is a strong overlap (p-value<10−100) between transcripts that were upregulated by emetine treatment in WT and ΔEDF1 lines at 30 and 120 min.
source: These observations are clarified by the strong overlap (p-value<10−100) between transcripts that were upregulated by emetine treatment in WT and ΔEDF1 lines at 30 and 120 min (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The transcriptional response to emetine is similar in WT and ΔEDF1 cells, but the levels are attenuated in ΔEDF1 cells.
source: the transcriptional response is similar, but the levels are attenuated in ΔEDF1 cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the RNA-seq data.

claim: EDF1 coordinates multiple responses of the ribosome-mediated quality control pathway.
source: Our results uncover mechanisms through which EDF1 coordinates multiple responses of the ribosome-mediated quality control pathway and provide novel insights into the intersection of ribosome-mediated quality control with global transcriptional regulation.
evidence: This is a summary statement from the abstract supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: EDF1 provides novel insights into the intersection of ribosome-mediated quality control with global transcriptional regulation.
source: Our results uncover mechanisms through which EDF1 coordinates multiple responses of the ribosome-mediated quality control pathway and provide novel insights into the intersection of ribosome-mediated quality control with global transcriptional regulation.
evidence: This is a summary statement from the abstract supported by the data presented in the manuscript.
